title: IT Support Lead: Triage an Office Connectivity Outage
prompt: You lead IT support for fictional Harbor Offices. At 10:00, six employees on the second floor report that both email and the internal booking page fail. The reception computer on the ground floor works. A meeting with visitors starts in 20 minutes. Company procedure allows documented non-disruptive checks; network configuration changes require the network on-call engineer. Prioritize diagnosis, continuity, and your handoff.
blurb: Narrow an office outage, coordinate authorized investigation, and keep an imminent meeting moving.

rubric.label: Narrow the failure
rubric.description: Uses scope comparisons to select a likely fault boundary.

anchors.0: Declares a global email outage or changes many devices without checking scope.
anchors.2: Compares affected and unaffected users and identifies a possible local network issue.
anchors.4: Uses floor, wireless-versus-wired, and multiple-service evidence to prioritize a network hypothesis while keeping other causes open.

rubric.label: Coordinate safe diagnosis
rubric.description: Escalates useful evidence and preserves authorized change control.

anchors.0: Reboots shared infrastructure or changes network settings without authorization.
anchors.2: Collects times and symptoms and contacts the network engineer.
anchors.4: Sends a concise timeline and change correlation, requests targeted authorized investigation, and avoids treating correlation as a confirmed cause.

rubric.label: Verify service and support users
rubric.description: Separates immediate continuity from verified restoration.

anchors.0: Closes the incident after one person reconnects or ignores the visitor meeting.
anchors.2: Offers the approved room and checks that affected services recover.
anchors.4: Assigns updates, tests multiple affected users and both services after mitigation, records residual issues, and confirms the meeting workaround with its owner.

reference.scenario: You lead IT support for fictional Harbor Offices. At 10:00, six employees on the second floor report that both email and the internal booking page fail. The reception computer on the ground floor works. A meeting with visitors starts in 20 minutes. Company procedure allows documented non-disruptive checks; network configuration changes require the network on-call engineer. Prioritize diagnosis, continuity, and your handoff.

facts.value: Affected employees are on the same Wi-Fi network; one reports wired access works. There are no reports from remote workers yet.
facts.reveal_when: candidate asks about network, scope, or wired-versus-wireless comparison

facts.value: A planned access-point update ended at 09:55, but no failure is confirmed. The network engineer is reachable; there is an approved visitor meeting room on the ground floor.
facts.reveal_when: candidate asks about changes, technical escalation, or meeting alternatives

model_points: The first useful distinction is localized connectivity versus application failure. The shared Wi-Fi symptom and working wired connection support a local network hypothesis; neither proves the update caused it.
Capture the start time, scope, error descriptions, and comparison results, then involve the network engineer. Do not ask employees to perform repeated disruptive changes or bypass network controls.

Offer the approved ground-floor room for the imminent meeting. Verify recovery with affected wireless users using both services, update the incident record, and carry unresolved questions into the handoff.

probes.trigger: candidate immediately rolls back the update
probes.question: What evidence connects the update to the failure, and who can authorize the change?
What happens to the visitor meeting during your investigation?

fair_alternatives: A permitted wired connection can be a temporary option for an individual if available; do not assume enough ports exist for everyone.
Escalating before finishing every comparison is reasonable when the impact is broad, provided the evidence is labeled incomplete.
red_flags: Declares a global email outage or changes many devices without checking scope.
Reboots shared infrastructure or changes network settings without authorization.
Closes the incident after one person reconnects or ignores the visitor meeting.
follow_ups: Write a short incident update with affected scope, leading hypothesis, next owner, meeting workaround, and a recovery check.
reference.exemplar_answer: I would check whether the affected people share a floor and connection type. Working reception and wired access suggest a local wireless problem, but I would not call the recent update the cause yet. I would send the network engineer the times and comparison results, ask for targeted investigation, and arrange the approved ground-floor room for the meeting. After mitigation I would check both services from several affected wireless devices before closing the incident.

interviewer_notes: Act as the support partner receiving requests for observations. Reveal the update only when asked about changes. Do not invent network outputs or require vendor commands. Use only supplied facts; say when something is unknown. Accept plain language and equivalent approaches. Assess the demonstrated decisions, not accent, confidence, credentials, or access to particular employers. This is a fictional exercise; do not imply real actions were performed.

learning_drills.title: Build an outage update
learning_drills.prompt: Write a short incident update with affected scope, leading hypothesis, next owner, meeting workaround, and a recovery check. This is self-guided practice; no model assessment is performed.
checklist: Define a check beyond one successful login
